caballinealoes.c: ABALLINE Alloes, is a courser sort, which being generally used by Farriers to purge Horses, is called by this Name of Caballine Aloes.

cableofaship.c: CABLE of a Shis, is (as is well known) a great Rope of 3 Strands, which being fastned to the Anchor holdeth the Ship last when she Rides. The Sea Terms about it are j i. The Cable is well laid, that is, is well wrought or made. r. Serve the Cable, or Plat the Cable, that is, bind it about with Ropes, Clouts, Ac. to keep it from galling in the Hawse. 3. To splice a Cable , is to make two Pieces last together by working the several Strands of the Rope one into another. 4. To Quoile the Cable, is to roll it up round in a Ring, ol which the leveral Roils one upon another are called Cable Tire. They lay Pay more Cable, that is, let it more out from the Ship, that the Boat which carries the Anchor may the more easily drop it into the Sea ; and sometimes they say, Pay chrap the Cable, (i. e.) put or hand it out a* pace. In the lame Sense as Pay more Cable, they lay also Veer more Cable, that is. hand or let more out. When two Cables are Ipliced together, 'tis called A Shott of a Cable.

cabosed.c: CABOSED ( Spanish ) the Trem in Heraldry for the Head of any Beasts being cut off just behind the Ears, by a Section parallel to the Face, or by a Perpendicular Section ; whereas Couping is usually expressed by an Horizontal one, and is never so dole to the Ears as Cabojing.

caburns.c: CABURNS (in a Ship) are Lines used to bind Cables withal; they are usually made of Rope Tarn or Spun Tarn,

cacatoriafebris.c: CACATORIA Febris, is an intermittent Fever (so called by the famous Sylvius ) accompanied with a violent Purging, which is sometimes griping, and very painful, extreamly afflicting, and weak ning to the Patient.

cachecticus.c: CACBECTICUS, is one that has an ill habit of Body.

cachexy.c: CACHEXY, is an ill habit of Body, proceeding from a bad Disposition of the Fluids and Humours ; whence Lingring Fevers, Consumptions, and Dropsies are contracted : In this Disease the Face is often pale and discoloured, and the Body big and swoln. Cachexia, taken also in a large Sense is opposite to siskin, and as a good Habit of Body is common to all found Parts, so an ill one is propagated by all the ill Parts. Strictly Cachexy is only taken for an ill Disposition of the Habit of the Body, and Euexia , on the contrary, for a good Disposition of the Humours, or Blood, and Body. Blanchard.

cacochymy.c: CACOCHYMY, is the abundance of ill Humours in the Blood ; and it is either Ulcerous, Bilious, Pituitous, Melancholick, Acid, Salt, or Sharp. Blanchard. j

cacoethes.c: CACOETHES, ChironiumVlcus, or Telephium ; is a Disease or Ulcer beyond cure, which is called a Malignant Vlcer ; this happens when an Ulcer is Callous, or Sinuous under which there sometimes lie little putrified Bones that have fallen down. Blanchard.

cadence.c: CADENCE, or Close, in Musick, is a kind of Conclusion of the Tune, which is made of all the Parts together, in divers places of any Key.

caducusmorbus.c: CADUCUS Morbus, or the Epilepsy, is a ConI vnlsive Motion of all the Parts of the Body, more ! especially, in the Hands and Feet, accompanied with a Deprivation of the Inward and Outward Senses.

ccumintestinum.c: CÆCUM Intestinum, the Blind Gut, so called because one end of it is shut up, insomuch that the Fæces and Chyle both come in and go out at the same Orifice. Its use in Man is obscure, as being very small and commonly empty.

calends.c: CALENDS ; so the Rgmans called the first Days of every Month, from the Greek word t&Kta, voco, to call ; because Anciently counting their Months by the Motion of the Moon, there was a Priest appointed to observe the Times of the New Moon ; who having seen it, gave notice to the President over the Sacrifices, and he called the People together, and declared unto them, how they must reckon the Days until the Nones, pronouncing 5 times the word kxmu, if the Nones happened on the jth Day, or 7 times if they happened on the 7th Day of the Month.

calibreorcaliper.c: CALIBRE or Caliper, is the Highest, or rather Diameter of a Piece of Cannon, or any Fire Arms ac the Mouth.

calipers.c: CALIPERS, is an Instrument made like a Sliding-Rule, to embrace the two Heads of any Cask, to find the Length. There is also the Gunners Callipers or CompaJJ'es for finding the Diameter of the Ball, and Bore of the Gun.

calipercompasses.c: CALIPER Compasses, are Compasses used by Gunners with crooked or bowing Legs, to mea T sure the Diameters of Bullets, and Cylinders of Guns.

callippickperiod.c: CALLIPPICK Period, was an Improvement of the Cycle of Meton of 19 Years, which Callippus a famous Grecian Astronomer, finding in reality to contain 19 of NabonaJJ'afs Years 4 Days and •-], he, to avoid Fractions, quadrupled the Golden Number, and by that means made a new Cycle or Period of 76 Years ; which time being expired, he supposed the Lunations ot Changes of the Moon would all happen on the lame Day of the Month, and Hour of the Day, that they were on 76 Years before.

callous.c: CALLOUS. A Swelling is said to grow Callous’, when ’tis hardened, as sometimes the Lips of a Wound. This is derived from

callus.c: CALLUS, is a kind of Swelling without Pain, like Skin contracted by too much Labour. Blanch ar d.

calva.c: CALVA, the Hairy Scalp, or upper part of the Head, which either by Disease or Old Age grows Bald first.

calx.c: CALX, in Chymistry, is that which is produced by Burning or Calcination (' which lee ) of any Metal or Mineral in a Crucible, £?'.

CALX, is the second Bone in that part of the Foot which succeeds the Ancle, bigger and stronger than the rest; oblong and grows backward, that a Man may stand more strongly upon it, and not fall so easily backward.
CAEX, also, is that which by Calcining is either turned into Alcoal, as Calx Saturni, or at least is made friable, as Harts-Horn burnt.

calxofgold.c:
CALX of Gold: Though it hath been look’d upon as a thing of great difficulty , yet the Noble Mr. Boyle tells us, that if you grind well together a thick Ama/gama of Gold and Mercury, with ac least an equal weight of finely powdered Sulphur, and then put the Mixture to sublime in a proper Glass, there will rile by degrees of Fire, a Cinnabar ;

CAN CAN nabar ; and this will leave behind it a finer Calx of Gold than is to be had by some far more difficult Processes. See, the Mechan. Product of Volatility.

calyx.c: CALYX, in Botany, signifies the Cup which contains or encloses the Flower in any Plant j and sometimes 'tis used tor the Flower it self when its Figure is like that of a Role, and not yet having its Leaves expanded.

cambring.c: CAMBRING; the Sea-men say a Deck lies Cambring when it doth not lie Level, but higher in the Middle than ar either End. Also it her Keel is bent in the Mid die upwards (which may happen from her lying a-ground on a place where neither her Aft nor Fore-part do touch it, and from many other Reaions taken from her make) they lay the is Cambet -keel’d.

campaign.c: CAMPAIGN, is a Military Term, signifying the Space of Tune during which Armies are maintains every Year in the Field. So a Man is said to have made twenty Campaigns, when he hath (pent so many Years in War-like Services in the Field.

campflying.c: CAMP Plying, is a strong Body of Horse and Foot commanded usually by a Lieutenant General, which is always in motion, both to cover our own Garrisons, and to keep the Adverse Army in continual Alarm. CANA L, is a Word frequently used by Anatomical Writers, to signify a Channel or Passage, through which any Juices or Fluids of the Body do slow.

canalicltlusarteriosus.c: CANALICLTLUS Arteriosus , is a Vessel betwixt the Arterious Veins in the Lungs, and the gteat Artery in the Fœtus ; for its obliterated in Adult Persons : its use in Foetus's is, that the Blood may be discharged by this Duttus out of the Arterious Vein, into the great Artery, because that the Blood is net accended in the Lungs, for want of Respiration in the Womb.

cancer.c: C ANCER, one ot the twelve Signs of the _?<>- dittos, drawn on-the Globe in the iorm of a Crab, and thus marked D. Through the beginning of this Sign pastes a Circle parallel to the Equinoctial, called the Tropics of Cancer, or the Northern Tropick ; to which Circle, when the Sun comes it makes the Summer Solstice , and is turning his course back again towards the Equinoctial.

caninafames.c: CANINA Fames, or Dogs-Appetite, is an inordinate Hunger attended with a Vomiting and a Looseness, which proceeds from a depraved Acts on of the Stomach, craving Food in a greater measure than Nature requires.

canini.c: CANINI, are two Teeth in each Jaw, one on each side of the Incisivi ; they are pretty thick and round, and they end in a sharp Point; they have' each one Root which is longer than the Roots of the Incijivi ; their proper use is to pierce the Alimenrs.

caninus.c: CANINUS, a Muscle of the Lip, serving to put the l ips upwards. CANIS Asa)or (st Minor , the greater and lesser Dog, are two Constellations of Stars drawn upon the Globe in Figure of this Animal; and the greater of them hath in his Mouth that vast Star called

caniculus.c: CANICULUS, or the Dog-star, which rising and setting with the Sun from about the 24th of July to the 28th of -August, gives occasion to that time which is usually very Hot and Sultry, to he called the Canicular or Dog-days.

cannamajor.c: CANNA Major : See Tibia, CANNA Minor See Fibula.

Canon also is the Word f° r the Tables of Logarithms, Artificial Signets, Ta#' gents, and Secants , which are of admirable in Trigonometry. ’Tis also the Name of a Surgeon's Instrument, which they make use of wh^ 1 they low up Wounds.

capiasprofine.c: CAPIAS pro fine, is, where one being by Judgr ment fined unto the King, upon the lame Offence committed against a Statute, doth not discharge it according to the judgment, for by this is his Body taken and committed to Prison until he content the King for his Fine.

capiasadsatisfaciendum.c: CAPIAS ad Satisfaciendum, is a Writ of Execution alter Judgment, lying where a Man recovers in an Action Personal, as Debts, or Damages, or Detinue in the King's Court; and lie against whom the Debt is recovered, and hath no Lands nor Tenements, nor sufficient Goods, whereof the Debt may be Jevy’d : lsor in this cafe, he that re r coveretli, iliall have this Writ to the Sheriff, commanding him, that he take the Body of him against whom the Debt is recovered, and he shall be put in Prison until Satisfaction made.

capiasutlcgntnm.c: CAPIAS utlcgntnm, is a Writ of Execution which lieth against him that is out-!aw’d upon any Suit, by which the Sheriff, upon the receipt thereof, apprehendeth the Party out-sawed, for not appearing upon the Exigent, and keepeth him in safe Custody till the return of the Writ, then bringeth him into Court, there further to be ordered lor his Contempt.

capiasutlegatum.c: CAPIAS utlegatum (3‘ Inr/uiras de bonis (3 catalUs, is a Writ all one. with the former, but Lc gives a farther Power to the Sheriff, besides the Apprehension of his Body, to enquire of his Goods and Chattels.

capiasinwithernamiumdehomine.c: CAPIAS in TVithernamium de ho mind , is a Writ that lieth for a Servant in Withcrnam.

capiasinwithcrnamdeaveriis.c: CAPIAS in Withcrnam de Averiis, is a Writ that lieth for Cattle mPJAthernam.

capillaments.c: CAPILLAMENTS, Capillamenta , arc those small Threads or Hairs ('whence the word) which grow up in the middle of a blower, and are adorned with little Knops at the Top : Those Knpps are called the Apices of a Flower ; and these CV,- pillaments are called the Stamina.

capillaryplants.c:
CAPILLARY Plants , are such as have no main Stalk or Stem, but grow to the Ground as Hairs to one’s Head, and which bear their Seeds in little Tuffs, Bunches, or Protuberances on the Back-side of their Leaves ; whence by some they are called Dorfipara and Tcrgifœtx, And these are either with an , Vndivided Leaf, as the IT.cmionitis and thd Phyllitis ; or with a Singly divided Leaf : and these have rhe Leaf either cut or jagged in, but not divided into Pinnae clear home to the main Rib; as Pohpodium, J.cn - chitis, Scolopcndria, Adi Ant hum, Acroftichcn Thai. . Or cllc divided quite home to the Rib, and. hanging like Pir.n.e ; as the Cham.efelix Marina and the Trichomancs . Others have the Leaf Dotibly divided, or at least once subdivided ; the first Division being into Branches, and the ad into Pinna ;; as the H.emionites Multifida, the Fihx mas, the Fiiix Pahtftris , Filix Saxatilis ; the Adiantum Album, and Nigrum. capillaryvessels.c: GAPILLARY Vessels, small Veins and Arteries, like Thread or Hairs.

capillation.c: CAPILLATION, according to some Writers, is a Fracture in the Skull, so small that it can scarce be found, which yet often proves mortal. CAP 1 TATÆ Plantat , in Botany , are such Plants whose Flowers are composed of many edged and hollow little Flowers; and Mr. Hay calls them by this Name, because their Scaly Calyx (or Cup of the Flower) most usually swells out into a large and round Belly, containing within it the Pappous Seed ; as Carduus, Centaury , Knapweed, Cinara, Cirfium, Lappa maj. Cyanus , &c.

capitalofabastion.c: CAPITAL of a Bastion, in Fortification, is a Line drawn from the Angle of the Polygon to the Point of the Bastion, or from the Point of the Bastion to the middle of the Gorge. These Capitals are from 35 to 40 Fathom long, that is to say, from the Point ot the Bastion to the Place where the two Demigorges meet.

capital.c: CAPITAL, or Chapitel, or Chapiter, signifies in Architecture, the Top of a Pillar; and this is different, according to the different Orders.

capite.c: CAPITE, is a Tenure that holds immediately of the King, as of his Crown, be it by Knightlervice or Soccage, and not of any Honour, Castle, or Mannor.

capitulum.c: CAP1TULUM, in Botanicks, is the Head or Flowring Top of any Plant, being composed of many Flowers and Threads (or Stamina) closely connected in a Globous, Circular or Discous Figure ; as the Flowers of Blew-bottles, Scabious, Carduus, 8cc.

caponniere.c: CAPONNIERE, in Fortification, is a covered Lodgment of about 4 or 5 Foot broad, encompassed with a little Parapet of above two Foot high, which serves to support the diverse Planks laden with Earth. This Lodgment is large enough to contain 15 or 20 Soldiers, and is usually placed upon the Extremity of the Counterscarp, having sometimes several little Embrasures made therein, commonly called Mardrejsts. They are generally on the Glacis, or in dry Moats.

caprsaltantes.c: CAPRÆ Salt ant es, is the Term for a fiery Meteor or Exhalation which sometimes appears in the Atmosphere, and is not fired in a strait Line, but with Inflexions or windings in and out.

capreolariavafa.c: CAPREOLARIA Vafa, in an Animal Body, are such as twine about like the Caprcoli or Tendrils of Vines.

capreolus.c: CAPREOLUS, in Botany, is the Clasp or Tendril, by which the Vines and such like creeping Plants fasten themselves to those things which are designed to support them.

capreolatplant.c: CAPREOLATÆ Pi ant a , are such Plants as turn, wind and climb along the Surface of the Ground by means of their Capreoli or Tendrils • OS Gourds, Cucumbers, Melons, &c.

capricorn.c: CAPRICORN, the Goat, one of the Zodiacal Signs marked thus, yp : Through the first degree of it the Southern Tropick, or the Tropick of Capricorn passes at 23°. 30'. distance from the Equator.

capstan.c: CAPSTAN, or as the French write it Cabestan, others Capstand, of a Ship, is of two kinds, the Main Capstan, and the Jeer Capstan. The Main Capstan is that Piece of Timber which is placed next behind the Main Mast, its Foot or lower end standeth in a Step, on the lower Deck; and its Head is between the two upper Decks. Its several Parts are thus called ; the smallest Part of it, the Spindle ; the Brackets set unto the Body of the Capstan, close under the Barrs, they call fa&Whelps. '-AR 1 NA, is a Term used both by the Anatonearly where the Subclavian Arteries arise ; here the Trunk begins to be divided into two Branches, which are tilde Carotides ; they ascend directly upwards (though the Right sometimes arises from the right Subclavian) and ac their rife are sustained by the T Lymus $ then having bestowed Twigs P or

CAR CAS on the Larynx, Tongue, the Muscles of the Os Hyoidcs, and the adjacent Glands, they pass up on cadi side by the sides of the Wind-pipe to the Faucet, together with the Internal Jugular Vein, and there are subdivided into the External and Internal Branches. The External is smaller, and is dispersed into all the Muscles of the Cheeks, Forehead, Temples, Lips; and in general, through all the outer parts or the Head and Face. The Internal, which is larger, fends first some more Twigs to the Ear jinx, Tongue, and to as also to the Glands behind the Ears, and the spongy parts of the Palate and Nose.- Then it entreth the upper Jaw, and bestows a small slip on the Root ot each Tooth (as the External did on the Roots of the Teeth of the lower Jaw) whereby sharp Humours flowing in upon them, sometimes cause a very painful Tooth ach. The remainder of it climbs upon the Skull, being about its Basis divided into two Branches; the less and hinder whereof having sent one slip to the inner Muscles of the Neck, and another through the hole of the uppermost Vertebra into the Membrane that invests the Spinal Marrow, ascending further enters the Skull at the hole by which the sixth Pair of Nerves ("commonly so called) comes out, and creeping along the Dura Mater, ends near its Sinus (which yet some say it enters.) The larger Branch, tending upwards, is carried through the bony Channel in the Wedge-like Bone with a winding Duct to the Sella Equina ; at whose Basis , aster it hath sent out a Twig on each side into the Dura Mater, it opens it self into many small Slips, which being interwoven with those ot the Cervical Artery (above-mentioned ) make the siete Aiirubile , which is more observable in Beasts than in Men ; yet it is not all spent on the said Slips, but perforating the Dura Mater , it enters the Pia Mater with two notable Branches, which being divided into very small Twigs are mingled with those of the Cervical Artery, with which they pass out of the Skull and accompany the Spinal Marrow even to the Loins. Afterwards it fends a small Branch through the second hole of the Wedge-like Bone with the Optick Nerve, out of the Skull to the Eye : And yet still supplying more Twigs to the Substance of the Brain and Pia Mater , and being united with some other Twigs of the Cervical Artery, it makes the Plexus Chore ides.

catapasma.c: CATAPASMA, a fragrant Powder which is sometimes applied to the Scrobiculus Cordis , to strengthen the Stomach.

cataphora.c: CATAPHORA, is the same with Coma j they only differ in this, that Cataphora is taken as the Genus to all forts of Stupors that afe not attendded with a Fever, Blanchard.

cataplasm.c: CATAPLASM, is a topical Medicine of the consistence of a Pulrise ; it is usually prescribed two ways, either boiled, or without it ; the former is more frequent, the latter of more efficacy : In the former, they are to take such Vegetables as are proper, as Roots, Herbs, Seeds, Flowers, Fruits, (sic. adding proper Meals, or omitting them; all which are boiled up in a convenient quantity of Liquor, v.g. Water, Beer, Al ilk, Honey, ( 3 c. to the consilience of a Pulrise: The latter is prepared commonly of Vegetables slued small with the infusion of so much Liquor only as may make it of the former Consistence. You may add here Meal, Crumbs of Bread, Oyls, Ointments, as in the former sort of Cataplasms. Blanchard.

cataptosis.c: CATAPTOSIS, is one Symptome of an Epileptic, when Men fall suddenly to the Ground. Blanchard.

cataract.c: CATARACT, a Disease in the Eyes, and is twofold, either beginning, as a Suffusion only, or confirmed, as a Cataract properly so called ; the Incipient isbut a Suffusion of the Eye when little Clouds, Motes, and Flics seem to fly before the Eyes; but the confirmed Catarall , is when the Pupil of the Eye is either wholly or in part covered, and shut up with a little thin Skin ; so that the Sun-beams have not due admittance to the Eye. Blanchard.

CATARACT, is a Precipice in the Channel of a River, caused by Rocks, or other Obstacles stopping the Courie of its Stream, from whence the Water falls with a great noise and impetuosity ; as the Cataralls of Nile, Danube, plane, 8cc,

This was proposed as a Problem by that excellent Mathematician M. cerebrum.c: CEREBRUM, the Brain, is strictly taken for the foremost part of the Substance, which is within the Skull; and it is a Substance of a fort peculiar to it self. Outwardly it is covered with the Skin called Pin Mater. It is wrought with many Turnings and Windings. Irs exreriour Substance is Ailty, wherein the Animal Spirits are thought to be generated : The Interior is white, which receives the Animal Spirits from the former, and discharges them by the Corpus Callofum, and the Aiedulla Oblongata into the Nerves, upon which voluntary Actions do chiefly depend. Likewise the Brain is the Subject of Imagination, Judgment, Memory, and Reminiscence ; for the Ideas or Species of things being received from the Organs of the External Senses, are carried to the common Sensory, or the beginning of the Medulla Obiongata, and then by the Corpora Striata, and the Corpus Callofum, there the Judgment and Imagination are probably formed ; but the Seat of the Memory is said to be in the Cortical part of the Brain, and is the Idea’s after some time chance to be called for out of the place of the Memory, then it’s properly said to be Reminiscence or Remembring Sleep is likewise transacted in the Brain $ concerning which sec in its proper place. chamade.c: CHAMADE, is a Signal made by the Enemy, either by beat of Drum or found of Trumpet, when they have any Matter to propound ; as when they found or beat a Parley.

chamber.c: CHAMBER ; that part of the Cavity of a great Gun where her Charge lies, is called the Chamber: Those Pieces which at Sea they call Afirthercrs, have Chambers which are put in at their Breeches.

chambranle.c: CHAMBRANLE.an Ornament in Masonry and Joyners Work. , bordering the three Sides of Doors, Windows, and Chimneys. It is different according to the several Orders, and consists of three Parts, viq_. the Top, called the Traverse, and the two Sides the Ascendants.

champarty.c: CHAMP ARTY (in Common-Law) signifies, a Maintenance of any Man in his Suit depending, upon condition to have part of the things (be it Lands or Goods) when recovered.

chancemedley.c: CHANCE-MEDLEY ( signifies in Law ) the casual killing of a Man, not altogether without the Killer's fault, though without an evil intent.

chandeliers.c: CHANDELIERS, in Fortification, are Woods en Parapets made of two upright Stakes six Foot high, which support divers Planks laid across one another, or Bavins filled with Earth. They are made rile of in Approaches, Galleries, and Mines, to cover the Workmen, and to hinder the Besieged from forcing them to quit their Labours.' The only difference between Chandeliers and Blinds, is, that the former serve to cover the Pio -1 nceis before, and the latter to cover them over Head.

chanel.c: CHANEL, in the Ionics Capital, is a part which is somewhat hollow under the Abacus after the Lift el, and lies upon the Echinus, having its Contours or Turnings on each side to make the Valuta's,

chaos.c: CHAOS: The ancient Ethnics Philosophers suppose the World to be formed at first out of a Chaos, that is, a dark kind of turbulent Anno sphere, or a disorderly System of Mixture of all f orts of Particles together, without any Regularity in any respect. This the Greeks called Ni-<-» fopad'af, and the Latins I{udis Indigestaquc Moles - It is probable enough, that the Notion came from Mojes, who says, the Earth was without form and void, and that Darkjicjs was upon the Face of the Abyss : Though he gives no farther Description of it, nor tells us whence it took its Original, and came into such a confused state. Mr. IVuiston in his late new Theory of the Earth, supposes the Ancient Chaos, the Origin of our Earth, to have been the Atmosphere of a Comet; for which new, though indeed all things considered, not improbable Assertion, he endeavours to make out by many Arguments, drawn from the Agrcemcnr which appears to be between them; Sec bis Theory, p. 69. So that according to him every Planet is a Comet formed into a regular and lasting Constitution, and placed at a distance from the Sun, revolving in a nearly Circular 0 » bit: And a Comet, is a Planet, either beginning to b e destroyed, or remade, char is, a chaos or a Plants unformed, or in its Primeval State, and placed as yet in an Orbit very eccentrical.

chapeau.c: CHAPEAU, in Heraldry, is a Cap of Dignity used to be worn by Dukes; ’tis of a Scarlet Colour, lined with Ermines, and on it, as on a fEreatb, the Crcjl of Noblemens Coats of Arms is born, and by it parted from the Helmet, which no Crest must touch immediately.

chapiters.c: CHAPITERS (in Law) signifies, a Summary or Content of such Matters as are to be enquired of, or presented before Justices in Eyre, Justice 5 of Assize, or of Peace, in their Sessions.

Proper Charges are called Ordinaries : Which See. Thus Guiilim , but Bloom calls those Charges on which Rewards and Additions of Honour are often placed in a Coat of Arms, such as Cantons, Quarters, Gyrtns, Flashy, &c.

chart.c: CHART, is a Draught projected for the use of Seamen, discovering the Sea-coasts, Sands, Rocks, and is sometime taken for the Nautical Compass.

chartapardonationisutlagari.c: CHARTA Pardonationis utlagariœ, is the Form of a Pardon for a Man that is outlawed.

charterparty.c: CHARTER-PARTY, is an Indenture of Covenants and Agreements made between Merchants and Sea-faring Men, touching their Affairs, or between Owners of Ships and the Masters or Commanders.

chicanry.c: CHICANRY, is a trickish and guileful Practice of the Law.

chiliads.c: CHILIADS ; so the Tables of Logarithms are frequently named by many Authors.

chiliogon.c: CHTLIOGON, a Regular Plane Figure of looo Sides and Angles ; of which, though the Eye can form no distinct view, we may have a very clear Idea in the Mind ; and can easily demonstrate that the Summ of all its Angles are equal to 1996 Right ones; for the Internal Angles of every Plane Figure arc equal to twice as many Right Angles as the Figure hath Sides; except those 4 which are about the Point in the Middle, from whence the Figure is resolved into Triangles.

chimesofanyclock.c: CHIMES of any Clock: How to calculate Numbers for them, and to fit and divide the Chime Barrel : See in Watch-wrk.

chiragra.c: CHIRAGRA, is a sort of Gout in the Hands only.

chirographer.c: CHIROGRAPHER, is he that in the Common* Picas, ingroifes Fines acknowledged in that Court into a perpetual Record, (after they are acknowledged and fully passed by those Officers by whom they are first examined) and that writes and delivers the Indentures, one for the Buyer, and another for him that sells, and makes another indented Piece, containing also the effect of the Fine, which he delivers over to the Cuilos Brevissm , which is called the Boot of the Fine. The Chirographcr also, or his Deputy, proclaims all the Fines in the Court every Term, according to the Statutes, and then repairing to the Office ot the Custos Brcvium, there endorses the Proclamations upon the Back-side of the Foot thereof, and always keeps the Writ of Covenant, as also the Note of the Fine. - CHIROMANCY, the same with Palmistry, is a pretended way of Divination, telling of Fortunes , presaging Futurities , or discovering the Tempers and Constitutions of Persons, by a Ridiculous Inspection into the Hand, and observation of Wrinkles and Strokes of the Skin.

chives.c: CHIVES, is the Botanmck Word by which our Mr. stay renders the Latin Apices: tlisich see. But Dr. Grew calls the Stamina on which the Apices are fixd, by this Name of Chives,

chlorosis.c: CHLOROSIS, or Morbus Virgineus, commonly Icterus Atbus or the Grccn-Jickr/cjs, seems to be a kind of Phlegmatick Pituicous Droplie, arising from an Obstruction of the Menses, want of Fermentation in the Blood, and Detention or Depravation of the Ferment in the Womb ; whereupon the Muscular Fibres being obstructed, they become Lazy and unfit for Action. choleramorbus.c: CHOLERA Morbus, is a depraved motion of the Ventricle and the Guts, whereby the Bilious Excrements are discharged in great plenty up-, Wards and downwards. Slanchard.

chologogues.c: CHOLOGOGUES,are Medicines which purge Choler, Sulphureous and Bilious Humours; as Rlubarb , Senna , &c.. according to the old Notion.

chondrosyndesmus.c: CHONDROSYNDESMUS, the joining or' uniting of the Bones by a Cartilage placed betwixt them.

CHROMATiCK, a Term in Mustek, being the second of the three kinds, which abounds in Semi-tones, and contains only the least Diatonical Degrees. It is recorded in History, that Timothern the Milesian first invented this sort of Mustek, in the time of Alexander the Great, and the Spartans banistted him by reason that being accustomed only to the Diatonic ^ kind , they judged the Chromatics to be too loir.

chrystalsofsilver.c:
CHRYSTALS of Silver, or Vitriol of the Alton, is an Operation in Chymistry, whereby the Body; of Silver is opened and reduced into the form ot a Salt by Spirit of Nitre. .’Tis done thus, Dissolve an Ounce or two of Silver in about three times the Weight of Aquafortis, or which is better, good Spirit of Nitre. Evaporate the Dissolution in a Glass Cucurbite and over a Sand-hear, till about i of the Liqubr is flown off, then let the Remainder stand without stirring it and it will shoot into Chrystals, which rake out, and when they are dry, keep them in a Viol well ' stopt. Those Chrystals are used to make’ an Esr z char.

C H Y C H Y char, by touching any part with them. They are also given Inwardly in Dropsies sometimes, from two to six Grains, and they will purge gently. The Purgative Quality in these Cbrystals (there being no such thing either in the Silver or the Spirit ot Nitre) must arise from the new Texture and Conformation of the Parts of both, happening from this Union of the Parts of the Silver with those of Spirit of Nitre. These CbrySlals may easily be revived into good Silver again, if you put them to dissolve, as they will readily do in a Vessel of hot Water, in the bottom of which you shall have laid a Plate of Copper ; the Silver will precipitate down in a white Powder, which gather, wash and dry, and then melt it in a Crucible with a little Salt Peter, 'twill run into good Silver of the same weight as at first.

chrystallineheavens.c: CHRYSTALLINE Heavens, in the Ptolemaic System were two. One served them to explain the slow Motion of the fixed Stars, and caused them (as they thought) to move one Degree Eastward in about 70 Years. The Second helped them out in solving a Motion, which they called the Motion of Trepidation or Libration ; by winch they imagined the Sphere to swag from Pole to Pole.

chrystallinehumouroftheeye.c: CHRYSTALLINE Humour of the Eye : See Humours.

chrystallization.c: CHRYSTALLIZATION, is an Operation in Chymistry, by which the Salts dissolved in any Liquor are made to shoot into little prettily figured Lumps or Fragments which they call Cbrystals, from their being pellucid or clear like Chrystal. In order to bringing the Salts duly to Chrystaliize , you must gently evaporate part of the Moisture ; for if there be too much Liquor in proportion to the Salt, it will not coagulate or chrystallize at all; and if there be too little, the Salts will all run into one another and not chrystallize regularly. The general Rule to know when enough of the Moisture is evaporated, is when a little Skin begins to be on the Surface of the Liquor.

chyle.c:
CHYLE, is a white Juice in the Ventricle and Intestines , proceeding from a light Dissolution and Fermentation of the Victuals, especially of their Sulphur and Salt, with which Edible things abound, and which by the Intervention of the Acid Humour in the Ventricle becomes white; for if you pour an Acid upon any Liquor that is impregnated with Sulphur and Volatile Salt, it presently turns Milky, as is obvious in preparing Milk of Sulphur, or the Resinous Extracts of Vegetables. Nay, Spirit of Harts-horn and of Soot, abounding with Volatile Salt, if it be mix’d with an Acid, or with but plain Water, grows to be of a Milky ColourAt last the Chyle after aCommixtion and Fermentation with the Gall, and the Pancreatic!^ Juice, either Volatile or Acid, passing the Latleal Veins , Lee. is mixed with the Blood. The Analogous White appearance of the Chyle, whether in the Stomach, or Intestines, and always in the Vena Lade a and Thoracic ^ Dud, may be seen in the Commixtures of divers Liquids, which separated exhibits no such Appearance ; nor is this Phenomenon any otherwise than a Transposition of Particles, whether by a Menstruum insinuating into them, dividing them into gross Globules, as an Acid into Sulphur, as Vinegar with Oyl, &c. or else by Precipitation, as when a Gummous or Resinous Body is dissolved in a Spirituous Menstruum , and mix’d with a Phlegm ; so Tincture of Myrrh and Benjamin, &c. make a milky appearance in common Water. The Longitudinal and Transverse Order of the Guts, are the Instruments by which the Peristaltick Motion of them is performed, which Motion is not only necessary for pushing their Contents forwards, but by Reciprocal Contraction of those Muscular Fibres of the Guts , and Apposition of their Connivent Valves, the Mouths of the Lacteals arc disposed to receive what is fitted for them ; hence it is we can by no means make any Fluid whatever pass from the Cavity of the Guts, into those Lacteal Vessels in a dead Animal, A further use of this Contraction of the Muscular Fibres of the Intestines, is to accelerate the Chyle in its progress in the Lacteals, till the Lympha derived from the Extremities of the Arteries of the Guts joyns with it ; which Conjunction is made in the Ladeals before they leave the External Surface of the Intestines. By this means the Progression of the Chyle is made towards the Mefenterick Glands, into whole Cells it is received, where it again mixes with a Juice brought in by the Arteries of each Gland ; which Juice or Lymphatick Liquor, not only farther dilutes the Chyle, like that from the Arteries of the Intestines, but adds a fresh Impetus, by which its Motion is farther carried on through the Vast Ladea sccundi generis ; ( arising our of each Mefenterick Gland, and discharging their Contents into the steccptaculum Chyli.) Here the Chyle meets and joyns with the Lympha sent through the Lymphatics Duds from the Inferiour Limbs and neighbouring Parts, whereby the Chyle is not only farther prepared ; but its Ascension is promoted in the Thoracick Ducts, whose several Divisions and Inosculations (like the Veins of the Testicles ) with its many Valves looking from below upwards, and advantageous situation between the great Artery and Vertebra of the Back, together with the Lymphsducts, discharging their Lympha derived from the Lungs and neighbouring Parts of the Thorax, does demonstrate the utmost Art still used in order to its Ascension towards the left Subclavian Vein, where meeting with the Refluent Blood of the Superiour Parts, passes with it through the descending Trunk of the Vena Cava, and joyns with the Refluent Blood of the Inferiour Parts in the Right Auricle of the Heart; whence its expelled by its Contraction into the Right Ventricle , when the Heart is in Diastole ; but by the Systole or Contraction of the Heart, it’s again driven out thence into the Arteria Pulmonaris, through whose Extremities, in conjunction

C I c C I N on wirh chose of the Vena Pulmonahs, it passes to the Left Auricle and Ventricle of the Heart, from | whence it’s again expelled in the Systole (as above) into the Aorta or Arteria Magna, by whose Branches it’s conveyed through the whole Field of the Bo-j dy : The 3 tricuspid Valves in the Right, and z .Mitral Valves in the Left Ventricle of the Heart opposing its return into the Veins, and the Semilunary Valves of the Arteria Pulmonaris and Aorta preventing its Ingress into the Ventricles are sufficient (when rightly considered) to demonstrate the necessity of a Circulation of this grand fluid called Blood. circleequant.c: CIRCLE Equant, in the Ptolctnaick. Astronomy, is a Circle described on the Centre ol the Equant ; its chief use is to find the Variation of the first Inequality.

circleofperpetualapparition.c: CIRCLE of perpetual Apparition, is One of the teller Circles parallel to the Equator , being described by any Point of the Celestial Sphere which toucheth the Northern Point of the Horizon, and carried about with the Diurnal Motion. All the Stars that are included within this Circle never set but are always visible above the Horizon And the

circleofperpetualoccultation.c: CIRCLE of perpetual Occultation, is another Circle at a like distance from the Equator, and contains all those Stars which never appear in our Hemisphere. But the Stars situated between these Circles incessantly rife and set at certain times. CIRCLES of Altitude : See Almicantcrs. CIRCLES of Declination on the Globe : So some Writers call the Meridians on which the Declina - tion or Distance from the Equator of any Planet of Star is accounted.

CIRCULATE, Circulation, in Chymistry, signifies the giving a Motion to Liquors contained in a double Vessel (chat is, when the Necks of two Vessels are excellently well luted one into another) excited by Eire and causing the Vapours to ascend and descend to and fro, which Operation is intended either to subtilise the Liquors, or else to open some hard Body that is mingled with them. The circulating Vessel is sometimes called a PelU cane, or a blind Alembics. ClRCULAT.ON oftheBlood, is that Motion of it which is produced by the continual Reciprocation cf the Pulse; whereby there is a constant Expulsion of the Blood from the Heart into the Arteries, and as constant and continual an Influx ot Blood into it out of the Cava ; and seeing the Vtna Cava from whence the Supply comes,is never drawn dry; nor on the other hand, the Arteries which receive the Blood from the Heart continually, are unduly swelled with it; it must necessarily follow ("as our great Harvey first plainly proved) that this Motion proceeds Circularly, and that the Blood is continually driven out of the Heart into the Arteries, and out of these into the Parts to be nourished ; from whence it is reset bed by the Capillary Veins, which carry it into the Larger, and these into the Cava , from whence it returns to the Heart again. The Reasons enforcing the Necessity of a Circulation of the Blood arc these. 1. The great Quantity of Blood that is driven out ot the Heart into the Arteries at every Pulse. For though the Ancients who knew not this Circulation, imagined, that only a drop or two was expelled by every Systole, which they were necessitated to suppose, to avoid the great Distension that the Arteries must be liable to, if any considerable quantity issued into them ; yet it is certain and demonstrable, that there must needs an Ounce or more be driven into them each time: For ( taking it for granted, that there is no other way for any Liquor to pass from the Stomach to the Kidneys but through the Heart, along with the Blood) feeing if some Men at some times drink three Pints of Drink, they shall piss it out again in half an Hour, yea more of Tunbridgc Water in that space ; and seeing Secondly, that there is commonly as much Blood as Serum , that flows to the Kidneys (selie Blood returning back by the E nul gent Veins) it is clear, that by the two Emulgents (which are none of the largest Arteries) there must pass in half an Hour, six Pounds of Liquor, all which must come from the Heart; and how much more then may we conceive to be driven through all the other Arteries that run through the whole Body ? The most usual Form for Citadels is that of a Pentagon, a Square being too weak, and an Hexagon too big.

civillaw.c:
CIVIL-LAW, is properly the peculiar Law of each State, Country, or City .- But what we usually mean by the Civil-Law, is a Body of Laws . composed out of the best of the Roman and Greci~ an Laws, and which was in the main received and observed throughout all the Roman Dominions for above twelve hundred Years. The Romans took the first Grounds of this Law from the Twelve Tables; which were Abridgments of the Laws of Solon at Athens, and of other Cities in Grcccc famous for Knowledge and Wisdom, to which they added their own Ancient Customs of the City of Rome. These written Laws were subject to vari-, ous Interpretations, whence Controversies arising, they were determined by the Judgment of the Learned ; and these Determinations were what they first called Jus Civile: After their several Cajcs were composed, which, lest the People should make them at pleasure, were fixed certain and solemn; and this part of their Law they called Abtiones Juris, Cafes at Law : And by the by, the Romans alto had their PlebiJ'cita, which were Laws made by the Commons without the Authority of the Senate. The Jus Honorarium, which was an Edict of some particular Magistrate: The Senatus Con/ultum, which was an Ordinance made by the sole Authority of the Senate ; and tbe Principalis Conliltutio , which was Enacted by the Prince or Emperor. These Laws grew by degrees to a vast number of Volumes; and therefore the Emperour Justinian commanded his Chancellour Trtbonian, with the Assistance of the other Eminent Lawyers of that Time, to reduce it to a perfect Body. Suidas and some others, reflect on Tribonian s Learning and Integrity in this great Work ; but no one can excuse his Hast and want of Care, for he did that in three Years time which the Emperour faith (in the Constitutions) he

C L A C L I: he could not have imagin’d would be effected in Jess thau Ten, For this Law had now been in practice above 1000 Years, and the Volumes of it were swelled to the prodigious Number of 2000, which ’twas impossible for Tribonian to read over in that time, much less to compare and digest them well. However this Body of Law is called the Digests or Pandetts . This Body of the Civil-Larv is divided into three Volumes, which are still remaining; vi%. the Pandctts or Digests , the Code, and the Institutes : Which see. Afterwards to these were added the Autbcnticks or Constitutions of Justinian , called also Novella: Which fee also under the word Authenticity.

clerkofthecrowninchancery.c: CLERK of the Crown in Chancery, is an Officer there, that by himself or his Deputy, is continually to attend the Lord Chancellor, or Lord Keeper, for special Matters of State, by Commission or the like, either immediately from his Majesty, or by order of his Council, as well ordinary as extraordinary: Also all general Pardons upon Giants of them at the King's Coronation, or ac a Parliament, the Writs of Parliament, with the Names of Knights and Burgesses, are returned into this Office. He hath also the making of special Pardons, and Writs of Execution upon Bonds of Statute Staple forfeited.

clouds.c: CLOUDS, are a Congeries of (chiefly) Watery Particles, drawn or lent out of the Earth in Vapour; which, when these Particles are very nearly placed to one another, appear dense and thick; but when they are more remote, are clear and bright, and sometimes almost Transparent. It hath been frequently matter os dispute amongst Naturalists, how these Clouds are suspended in a Medium which must be lighter specifically than themselves. But ’tis easie to conceive, that the Parts which compose Clouds are so many little Bubbles, having a watery Skin over a little Sphere of fluid Matter lighter than Air, and therefore may easily, like the Bubbles of Soap and Water which the Children blow up with a little Pipe, be supported by the Air: But whenever they, are broken by the violent Agitation of Winds, or are driven against the sides of Hills, &c. they must change their form of Bubbles and fall down in Rain. See the word Vafour. Mr. Boyle faith an excellent Astronomer assured him, That though he had many times accurately.measured the Height of the Clouds , yet he could never find any (even white ones) to be above | of a Mile high, and few did exceed half a Mile.

cloyed.c: CLOYED: The Seamen say, when any thing is gotten into the Touch-hole of a great Gun, so that they cannot with a Primhtg Iron make way for the Powder to be put in to prime her, they say the Touch-hole is cloyed ; wherefore when Guns are nailed, 8cc. they say they are Cloyed.

clydon.c: CLYDON, is a Fluctuation of the Ventricle.

clypeiformis.c: CLYPEI-FORMIS , a sort of Comets resembling a Shield : See Dijcus.

clyssus.c: CLYSSUS, among some Chymists, is a long Digestion and Union of Oily Spirits (especially Mineral ones) together, in order to make a Composition or accurate Mixture of them. Sometimes tis taken for an Extraction and Union of the more subtile Parts of any Plant, Vid. fflfink, C hym. Lib .3. §. z. Schroder, lib. 3, c. 17. Sometimes for a Medicine made of the most active and energetical Parts of any Ingredients. COACERVATE Vacuum See Vacuum.

coach.c: COACH, the Council-Chamber on board a Flagg-Ship.

coalition.c: COALITION, is the gathering together and uniting into sensible Masses, the minute Corpuscles which compose any Concrete or Natural Body. Coalejcency is commonly taken for the same.

coamings.c: COAMINGS, aboard a Ship, are thole Planks, or that Frame, which raises up the Hatches higher than the rest of the Deck, in which Loop-holes for Muskets to (hoot out at, are usually made, in order to clear the Deck of the Enemy, when » Ship is Boarded.

coasting.c: COASTING, is that part of Navigation where the Places assigned are not far distant, so that a Ship may Sail in sight of Land, or within soundings between them. For the performance of which there's only required good knowledge of the Land, the use of the Compass, and Lead or Sounding-Line ; such are the Voyages on the Narrow or Britif)j Seas, between England, Holland, and France, alio all about the Balticl^Scas, and those in the Mediterranean are little else.

coat.c: COAT, by Anatomists, is taken for a Membranous Cover of any part of the Body; as the Coats of the Eyes, Nerves, Arteries, (3 c.

coats.c: COATS , in a Ship , arc pieces of Tarred Canvase which are put about the Masts at the Partners ; they ate also put about the Pumps at the Decks. that no Water may go down there ; and these are also used ac the Rudder's Head. COCCYGIS OS, is a Cartilaginous kind of Bone joined to the Extremity of the Or Sacrum ; it is composed of three or four Bones, of which the lower is still less than the upper till the last end in a small Cartilage, and it resembles a little Jail turned inWards .-It's use is to sustain the /(rHum Ifitefli'mtm ; it yields to the pressure of the f -'retus in Women in Travail, and therefore Midwives use to thrust it backwards, but sometimes they do it so ruddy and violently, that it occasions very great Pain, and several bad Effects. It’s called Os Coccygis because 'tis in shape something like a C vclyve's Bill; it's Bones are spongy and loft, and have neither Process nor Cavity, for the Spinal Marrow descends no farther than the bottom of the Os Sacrum, which terminates in the first Bone of the Os Coccygis.

cochlea.c: COCHLEA, is a Cavity of the inner part of the Ear, so called from its windings and turnings, for it has 5 or 4 Rings which mutually succeed one another ; it is girt about with a very soft and thin Membrane: See Ear .

cockpit.c: COCKPIT, in a Man of War, is a Place oh the fewer Floor or Deck abaft the moist Capstan, lying between the Platform or Orlop and the Steward’s Room, where are Subdivisions or Partitions for the Purler, the Surgeon, and his Mates.

cockswainorcoxon.c: COCK SWAIN or Cockjon , is an Officer aboard a Man of War who hath the care of the Barge or Shallop, and all things belonging to it; to be always ready with his Boat’s Gang or Crew, and to man the Boat on all occasions: He firs in the Stern of the Boat and Steers ; and he hath a Whistle to call and to encourage his Men.

coelum.c: COELUM, is the Cavity of the Eye towards the Corners. The Palate is also called Cesium by some. Elanchard.

coffer.c: COFFER, in Fortification, is a hollow Lodgment athwart a dry Moat from six to seven Foot deep, and from sixteen 10 eighteen broad, the upper part being made of Pieces of Timber raised two Foot above the Level of that moat; which little Elevation hath Hurdles laden with Earth for its covering, and serves as a Parapet with Embrasures. The Besieged generally make use of these Coffers to repulse the Besiegers when they endeavour to pass the Ditch, and they are distinguished only by their Length from the Capormieres which are likewise somewhat less in Breadth: And it differs from the Taver/e and Gallery, in that these are made by the Besiegers , and the Coffer by the Besieged. To save themselves from the Fire of these Coffers, the Besiegers Epaule, or th sow up the Earth on that side towards the Coffer.

In the Law, ’tis the Acknowledgment of a Fine, or confession of a thing done ; as also a Power or Jurisdiction : Thus Cognisance of Pleas is an Abilitv to call or cause a Plea out of another Court; which no one can do but the King, unless he cart shew a particular Charter for ir.

cohhsionofthepartsofmatter.c: COHHSION of the Parts of Matter, is that Quality from whencesoever arising, by which the Parts of all solid Bodies stick or adhere to one another: Some will have this to be effected by a certain Glue or Cement; others by the Particles being hooked and branchy, and so to catch hold of one another z others will have it to be occasioned by an Imaginary Funicutus or Invisible Rope or String which holds the Parts together ; others by bare Rest only; all which the famous fames Bernoulli in his Book de Gravitate Ætbcris, endeavours to refute, and thinks ’tis occasioned by rhe Pressure of the Incumbent Air or Æther and near the Earth of the whole Atmosphere. This Items to be confirmed by the known Experiment of the Cohesion of two well-posited Marbles together, which yet will easily and speedily fall asunder, when put into the exhausted Receiver, where the External Pressure of the Air is taken off; and Bernoulli supposes the whole Body ot the Æther as well as of the lower Air to gravitate continually upon the Earth, and by that means to keep all its Parts together.

cohobate.c: COHOBATE, a Term in Chymistry, implying a repeating the Distillation of the same Liquor, having poured it again on the Matter which remains in the Vessel. This Operation is used to open Bodies, or to volatilize the Spirits, and is called Cohobation.

coindications.c: COINDICATIONS, are Signs which do not indicate by themselves alone, but together with other Things, Circumstances, t$c. help the Physician to form a Judgment.

The Expaniion of Water in Freezing is about part ot the Space more than it before took up. The Expansive Force of Gold is so great, that if the Barrel of a Gun be filled with Water, and then have its Muzzle and Touch-hole well stopt, the Water within the Barrel when either by Natural Cold or a Freezing Mixture, it is turned into Ice, will break the Barrel in several places, as Mr. Boyle and many others have try’d. That Noble Philosopher contrived several Experiments to estimate or measure the Quantity of rhis Expansive Force, which were made with a Brass Cylinder ot two or three Inches in Diameter, into whose Cavity was put a Bladder filled with Water and strongly ty’d about the Neck, and over it was put a Wooden Plug to stop up the upper Orifice of the Cylinder, and on the Plug was put a broad flat Board, on which was laid as much Weight as one rime amounted to above an hundred Pound ; another time to an hundred and twenty Pounds; and another time to two hundred fifty four Pounds; and yet in all the Experiments, when the Water in the Bladder was turned into Ice, it expanded so as to raise up all this Weight very conspicuously, as appeared by a Circle designedly made on the Wooden Plug. He tells us also, that by mingling together z Saline Bodies, each of them purified by the Fire, though there did arise a very great Commotion, Hissing and Explosion, yet a very considerable degree of Cold was thereby produced ; and tho* he was under an Obligation of not discovering what these Ingredients were, ye he gives a Succedaneum to that Experiment, by telling us, that by putting good Salt of Tartar into Spirit of Vinegar, there was a Struggle, Commotion, and Hissing produced, and yet instead of Heat, as is usual in such Cases, a very sensible degree of Cold was produced. Sylivius also acquaints us with a Method of producing Cold by mingling Spirit of Vitriol with anorher Saline Spirit, If into 3 or 4 times its weight of Water, you put about half a Pound of Sal Armani ac I ( powdered, and stir it about to hasten the Dissolution, so great a degree of Cold will, even in the Heat of Summer, be produced, as is very surprising ; for if you nimbly shake it, or stir it about, it will produce actual Ice on the outside of the Glass, if you purposely wet it with Water. This noble Experiment Mr. Boyle first made, and thereby plainly proved the Mechanical Producibleness of the Quality of Cold ; and the Experiment may be of great use to cool Wine, &c. in the hot Months, or in such places where no good Ccllerage is to be had, The Sal A> maniacs, by evaporating the Water from it, may be recovered again, and will serve many times for the lame Experiment. COLOUR, may be considered two ways, 1, As it is a Quality redding in the Body that is laid to be so and so coloured, or which doth modify the Light alter such and such a manner.- Or 2. As more properly, the Light it self which 10 modified strikes upon the Organ of Sighs, and produces that Sensation which we call Colour. The Peripateticks assert Colours to be real Qualities, and inherent in the coloured Bodies, and suppose that Light doth only discover them, but not any effect of their Production. Plato thought Colour to be a kind of Flame consisting of most minute Particles, very congruous to the Pores of the live, and darted against it from the Object. And some Moderns will have Colour to be a kind of Internal Light of the more lucid parts of the Object, darkened, and consequently altered by the various mixtures ol the le!5 Luminous Parts. Others, as did some of the Ancient Atomists, maintain Colour not to be a Lucid Stream, but a Corporeal Effluvium issuing out of the coloured Body. Others account for all Colours out of the various mixture of Light and Darkness ; and the Cliymists sometimes will have it arise from the Sulphur and sometimes from the Salt that is in Bodies ; and some also from the third Hypostatick Principle, Mercury. The Cartesians , who make the Sensation of Light to be the Impulse made en the Fye by certain solid but very minute Globules easily permeating the Pores of the Air and Diaphanous Bodies. These, I lay, derive Colour from the various Proportion of the direct Progrcls or Motion of these Globules, to their Circumrotation or Motion round their own Centres; by which means they arc qualified to strike the Optick Nerve after distinct and divers manners, and so do produce the Perception of various Colours. Dr. stool^ in his Micrographs a says, The Phantasm of Colour is caused by the Senlatjon of the oblique or uneven Pulse of Light; and that this is capable of no more Varieties than two, which arifeTrom the two sides ot the Oblique Pulse ; so that there is in reality but two simple Colours, Yellow and Blue ; from the Mixture of which, and a due proportion of Black and White (that is* Darkness and Light) all Colours may be produced. The incomparable Mr. If. Kcxvton found by two Experiments on Prisms, that there is a great difformiry in the Rays of Light ; and that hereby the Origin of Colours may be unfolded. The Doctrine therefore of Colours accbrding to his Notion and Experiments are contained in the following Propositions. 1. As the Rays of Eight differ in degrees of Rcfrangibility, so they also differ in their Disposition to exhibit this or that particular Colour. Colours arc not Qualifications of Light, derived from Refractions, or Reflections of Natural Bodies (as 'tis generally believed) but Original and Connate Properties which in divers Rays are divers. .Some Rays are disposed to exhibit a Red Colour and no other; some a Yellow and no other; some a Green

COL COL a Green and no other; and so of the rest. Nor are there only Rays proper and particular to the more eminent Colours, but even to all their intermediate Gradations. 2. To the same degree of Refrangibility ever belongs the lame Colour, and to the lame Colour ever belongs the same degree of Refrangibility. The least Refrangible Rays are all disposed to exhibit a Red Colour, and conn rarity those Rays which are disposed to exhibit a Red Colour, are all the least Refrangible ; so the most Refrangible Rays are all disposed to exhibit a deep Violet Colour, and contrarily those that are apt to exhibit such a Violet Colour are all the most Refrangible: And so all the intermediate Colours in a continued Series belong to intermediate Degrees of Refrangibility. And this Analogy ’twixt Colours and Refrangibility, is very precise and strict z the Rays always either exactly agreeing in both, or proportionably disagreeing in both. The Species of Colour, and degree of Refrangibihty proper to any particular sort of Rays, is not mutable by Refraction, nor by Reflection from Natural Bodies, nor any other Cause that could be yet observed when any one sort of Rays hath been well parted from those of other kinds, it afterwards obstinately retained its Colour notwithstanding all endeavours to change it. Though refracted with Prisms, and reflected with Bodies, which in Day-light were of other Colours ; having also intercepted it with the coloured Film of Air interceding two compressed Plates of Glass; transmitted it thro' other coloured Mediums, and thro' Mediums irradiated with other sorts of Rays, and divers ty terminated it ; and yet could never produce any new Colour out of it. It would by contracting or dilating become more brisk or faint, and by the loss of many Rays, in some Cafes, very obscure and dark; but could be never seen to change in specie. 4. Yet seeming Transmutations of Colours may be made where there is any mixture of divers sorts of Rays ; for in such Mixtures the Component Colours appear not, but by their mutual allaying each other, constitute a middling Colour ; and therefore, if by Refraction, or any other of the aforesaid Causes, the Difform Rays, latent in such a Mixture, be separated, there shall emerge Colours different from the Colour of the Composition ; which Colours are not new generated, but only made apparent by being parted; for if they be again intirely mixt and blended together they will again compote that Colour, which they did before separation. And for the same reason, Transmutations made by the convening of divers Colours are not real; for when the Difform Rays are again fevered, they will exhibit the very same Colours, which they did before they entered the Composition ; as you see Blue and Yellow Powders, when finely mixed, appear to the naked Eye Green, and yet the Colours ot the Component Corpuscles are not thereby really transmuted but only blended ; for when viewed with a good Microscope, they still appear Blue and Yellow interspersedly. 5. At what time the Vapour ascends from the Head to the Extremity of the Tail, may be almost discovered by drawing only a Right Line from the end of the Tail to the Sun, and then noting the place where that Right Line cuts the Trajectory : For the Vapour in the extremity of the Tail, if it ascend in a Right Line from the Sun, will begin its ascent at the time when the Head of the Comet is in the place of Intersection. But indeed the Vapour doth not ascend in a Right Line front the Sun, but by retaining the Motion of the Comet which it had before its ascent, and compounding it with the Motion of its Ascent,it ascends obliquely ; wherefore it will be a truer Solution of the Problem , to suppose the Right Line which intericcts the Orbit, to be parallel to the length of the Tail, or rather (because of the Curvilinear Motion of the Comets ) that it diverge from the Line of the Tail. By this means I found that the Vapour which was in the extremity of the Tail, Jan. 25, began to ascend from the Head before December n, and therefore had taken up more than 45 Days in its Ascent: But all that long Tail which appeared Decemb. 10. ascended in the space of those two Days, which were then just past since its Perihelion ; wherefore the Vapour at the beginning, when the Comet was near the Sun a trended prodigiously swift, and afterwards continued to ascend with a Motion retarded by the Gravity of the particles, and by that ascent encreascd the length of the Tail: But the Tail, as long as it appeared, consisted almost ail of that Vapour which ascended from the time of the Perihelion ; and the Vapour which first ascended and composed the Bounds of the Tail, did not vanish till it was both too far off the Sun to be illuminated by him, and off us, to be visible. confiscate.c: CONFISCATE, in l aw, signifies, to be forfeited to the Publick Fffque, or King’s Treasury; For among the Ppmans the Emperour’s Treasure was kept in Hampers or Baskets, which in Latin is Fijcus. Now if a Man be indicted for feloniously stealing the Goods of another, though in truth they are the proper Goods of the Person indicted , yet if when the Goods are brought in Court against him, as the manner is, he shall then disclaim them; he doth by this DiscUimure lose the Goods, although he be afterwards acquitted of the Felony, and they shall be confiscated to the King ; but it is otherwise if he does not disclaim them. The same Law is, where Goods are found in the Felon’s possession, which he disavows; and afterwards is attainted of other Goods, and not of them, there the Goods which he disavows are confiscated to the King; but had he been attainted of the same Goods, they should have been said to be forfeited, and not confiscated, notwithstanding his Dilavowmenr. So if an Appeal of Robbery be brought, and the Plaintiff leaves out some of his Goods, he shall not be received to enlarge his Appeal; and forasmuch as there’s none to have the Goods so left out, the King shall have them a i Confiscate, according to the old Rule, Quod non capit Chris us, caps Fijcus.

conglobate.c: CONGLOBATE, a word used for such of the glands in an Animal Body as are smooth in their Surface, and seem to be made up of one conti nucd Substance. They serve to separate the Lympha from the Arterious Blood, and to return it by the Lympheducts, either into the Chyliferous or §anguiserous Vessels, though some think, the G.ends of the Mesentery, and Breasts of Lactetcent Women serve to separate true Chyle.

conglomerateglatids.c: CONGLOMERATE Glatids, are such in an Animal Body as are uneven in their Surface, and are made up as it were of many lesser Glands. Their use in the Body is to separate several sorts of juices from the Blood, and also to elaborate and alter them, and by proper Ducts to convey them to their appropriate Receptacles and Cavities. Thus the Parotides and Maxillary Glands separate and bring the Saliva into the Mouth by their proper Ducts.

Congruity, by the Naturalists is esteemed a Relative Property of a Fluid Body, whereby any part of it is readily united with any other parr, either of it self, or of any other Similar Fluid or Solid Body. And Incongruity is a Property by which it is hitidred from uniting with any Solid Or Fluid Body dissimilar to it.

contagion.c: CONTAGION, the communicating or transferring of a Disease front one Body to another, by certain Steams or Effluvia transmitted from the Body of the Sick Person. Some Diseases are Contagious, by immediate contact or touch, as the Madnesses a Dog, which is communicated by biting ; and the Venom of the French Pox, which is transmitted from the infected Person in the Act of Copula', ion, sometimes the Contagion is propagated by infected Cloths, as in the Itch, and Leprofie. And there are some Contagions that are transmitted thro’ the Air to a considerable distance, as the Plague, and other Pestilential Distempers; in which Case the Air is said to be Contagious that is full of Contagious Particles or Effluvia.

convexity.c:
CONVEXITY, signifies any Protuberancy or Swelling out of any thing, as Glasses are said to be Convex when they are thicker in the middle than at the Edges : or rather, when their Surface rises up regularly (so Vitelio Defines it j above the Plane of the Base as they are Concave, when the Surface sinks down regularly, or with a Regular Curvity below it; so that the same thing may be, and often is Concave within, and Convex without. Bb * Here

CON COP Here follow some Properties of Convex Glajset. i. If an Object be in the Focus of a Convex Glass, and the Eye on the other side the Glass, the Object will appear erect and distinct. %. If any Object be in the Focus of a Convex Glass, and the Eye in the opposite Focus on the other side, it will appear under the lame Angle, as it the Eye were in the Place of the Glass, and consequently the distance being double in that Position of the Eye and Object , it will appear thro’ the Glass magnified under an Angle almost double ef what it would appear to the Naked Eye. But the Eye can fee no more of its Area than the Breadth of Glass will permit. Mr. Molyneux in his Dtop trica Nova, shews how to determine the visible Area of an Object ia the Focus of a Convex Glass, from the distance of the Object, and of the Eye from the Glass, and the Glasses Breadth. P. 126. Prop, 34. 3. Is an Object be farther from a Convex Glass than the Focus, and the Eye on the other side be nearer than the distinct Bale of the Glass, it will lee the Object erect but confused, and it will be most confused when the Eye is placed in the distinct Bale. 4. But if the Object being placed as before, the Eye be farther from the glass than the distinct Bale, it begins to see the Object Inverted, and at a due Distance Distinct. 5. An English Convocation, or Synod , as it now stands for the Province of Canterbury , consists of a President, (the Lord Archbishop) and X1 Bistoops, li Deans, 53 Archdeacons, 24 Proctors of Chapters, 44 Proctors for the Diocesan Clergy, (2 for each Diocese) and one Pracentor. It is cloathcd with a little Membranous Bag , called the Pericardium , wherewith it is joyned to the Mediastinum, and the Diaphragm ; its Basis is upwards, and Point downwards, and it is placed in the Middle of the Chest, amongst the Lobes of the Lungs. corrugantmuscles.c: CORRUGANT Muscles, according to some, ate thole that help-to knit the Brows when one frowns; but they seem to be only a part of the Frontal Muscles that have their Fibres running in this place somewhat obliquely.

corrugatorsupercilii.c: CORRUGATOR Supercilii, is by some Anatomists reckoned as a Muscle of the Eyebrows, helping to knit them when we frown ; but it (eems to be only a parr of the Frontal Muscles, having. Fibres running in this place a little obliquely.

corruption.c: CORRUPTION, is the Destruction, Extinction, or at least the Cessation for a time, of the proper Mode of Existence of any Natural Body : For whenever any Body soles all or any of thole Accidents which are essentially necessary co the constituting it of such a kin.d, it is then laid to be corrupted or destroyed, and loses its former Denomination, being nor now a Body of the kind it was before. But as in Generation nothing Substantial is produced, so here nothing Substantial is lost or destroyed, but only that Modification of the Body which was its Form, and made but of such a Species.

corticalpartofthebrain.c: CORTICAL part of the Brain, is the outward Substance of the Brain, full ot Labyrinths and Meanders in the ous-side; it is covered with a thin Skin, and is of an Ash-grilly Colour, being, as Malprghius faith, only an heap of little Oval Glands, and full of little Vessels; inwardly the Medullary Substance is next to it. Its ule is thought by some to be the generating ot Animal Spirits from the Blood, and hence they are conveyed by the Medullary Sub dance to the Nerves, and distributed through the whole Body.- And the Seat of the Memory, and Sleep is placed there by many Anaromists.

cortin.c: CORTIN, in Fortification, signifies the Wall or Distance between the Flanks of two Bastions.

coruscationorflashing.c: CORUSCATION or Flashing, is (by the Cartesians ) an Exhalation spread under a Cloud , which rustling downwards, is let on Fire and flalheth.

corvus.c: CORVUS, a Southern Constellation in the Heavens consisting of 7 Stars.

corymbus.c:
CORYMBUS, in general, signifies the top of any thing j but among the old Writers about Plants, Corymbi were the Bunches or Clusters of 1 - vy Berries .- Some also call the top of the Stalk of a Plant, when 'tis so subdivided and adorned with Flowers or Fruits that its makes a round Spherical Figure by this name Cvrymbus , as the Tops of I.eeks, Onions, and of the Sambucus Aquatica, &c. and others confound the word witb'Lsolella, which expresses the Flowry Top of such Plants as have their Branches and Flowers spread round into the form of what our Women now call an Vmbrella ; Bur among our Modern Botanists it is used for a compounded difeous Flower, whole Seeds are not Pappous, or do not fly away in Down; such are the Flowers of Daisies, Com Mary-Gold, &c. And therefore the Acurate Botanist Mr. Bay, makes one large Genus of Plants to be such as have a Compound Difeous Flower, but without any downy Wings to carry off their Seeds, and these he properly calls, Corymbiferous Plants, and these he distinguishes into 1. Such as have a Radiate Flower, as the Flos Solis, Calendula , C alt ha, Flos Africanus, Chrysanthemum Segetum, Buthphnlmum,Ptearrmica, C C Absinthium,

COS. cas Absinthium TJmlfiliferum, Miliefolium, Bellis Major & Minor , Parthcntum, Chamameltim, &C. L. Such as havea Naked Flower/as the Abrotanum Fxmina, Eupatorium Cannabinum fxmina , Cojlui tloriorum, Ageratum , Absinthium, Ai timijia, Ace. To which he adds such' as he calls 'Corymbifiris Ajjines, i. e. such Plants as seem akin to the Corymbiferous kind, as Scablofa, Dyfjacus , Carduus , Spharocephalus, Eryngium, &c..

coryphe.c: CORYPHE, is the Crown of the Head; also the interior Extremity of the Fingers, near .the Nails. Blanchard,

coryza.c: CORYZA, or Gravedo , is' a Defluxion of a sharp, lair, and thick Humour, into the Mouth, Lungs, and Nostrils, from the Ventricles of the Brain, by the Olfactory Nerves ; for when it grows thick, it can neither be Percolated by the Reins, nor pass from the Pituitary Glandule through the Jnfundibulum into the Veins, and therefore it distils into the Nostrils by the aforesaid Nerves. Blanchard.

cosecant.c: CO-SECANT, is the Secant of an Arch which, is the Complement of another to 90 0 . CO-S 1 NE, is the Right Sine of an Arch, which is the Complement of another to 90 Degrees.

cosenageorcognatione.c: COSENAGE or Cognatione, is a Writ that lies where the great Grand-father is seized in his Demeso, as of Fee, at the Day ok his Death, of certain Lands and Tenements, and dieth, and then a Stranger entreth, and abateth ; for then llia$ his Heir have this Writ of Cosinage.

coshering.c: COSHERING, in the Feudal Laws j as there were many Privileges inherent by Right and Custom, so. were there several then grievous Exactions imposed by the Lords, by a sort of Prerogative or Scignioral Authority, as to lie and feast themselves and their Followers (call’d Costxring) at their Tenants House?. .

cosmeticks.c: COSMETICKS, are Medicines which whiten and soften the Skin, or in general, any thing that helps to promote the external Beauty, or good Apr pear ance of the Person that useth it.

cosmical.c: COSMICAL, a Term in Astronomy, expressing one of the Poetical Risings of a Star, for a Star is said to rife Cosmically when it riseth together with the Sun, or with that degree of the Ediptick. wherein the Sun then abides; and the Qosmical Setting, is when a Saar setts, of goes down 1 in the West at the same time as the Sun rises in the East.

cosmography.c: COSMOGRAPHY, is a Description of all the several Parts of the visible World, delineating them according to their Number, Positions, Morions, Magnitudes, Figures, and their other Properties. The two Parts of which are Astronomy and Geography.

cosseandcojstck.c: COSSE and Cojstck, the old word for Algebra.
