covine.c: COVINE, fin Law) is a deceitful Aiicnt or Agreement between two or more, to the prejudice of one another.

count.c: COUNT, (in Law) signifies as much as the Original Declaration in a Process, chough more used in Real than in Personal Actions, as Declaration is more apply’d to Personal than Real.

countwheel.c: COUNT-WHEEL, is a Wheel in the striking f art of a Clock, moving round once in 12 or 24 lours: It is by some called the Locking FJ-%ccl, because it hath commonly 1 1 Notches in it ar unequal distances from one another, in order to make the Clock strike 1, 2, 3, 4, &c. ’cis driven round by the Pintail of Import.

counterapproaches.c: COUNTER-APPROACHES, in Fortification, are Works made by the Besieged to hinder the Approach ot rhe Enemy, and when they design to attack them in form.

counterbattery.c: COUNTER-BATTERY, is one raised to play against another.

counterbreastwork.c: COUNTER-BREAST-WORK, a Term in Fortification, the same with False Bray.

counterchanged.c: COUNTER-CHANGED, is a Term in Heraldry , when there is a mutual changing of the Colours of the Field and Charge in an Escutcheon, by reason of one or more Lines of Partition, Thus in the Coat of the Famous Chaucer, he beareth Party per Pale, Argent and Gules, a Bend Counter-changed; i.e. that part of the Bend which is in that side of the Escutcheon which is Argent; is Gules, and that part of it which is iri the other side, is Argent.

countercomponed.c: COUNTER-COMPONED, the Heralds Term for a Bordure , or any Ordinary which hath two Rows only of Checkers of two different Colours ; but when it hath thfee or more, they call ic Cheeky.

counterforts.c: COUNTER-FORTS, are certain Pillars, and parts of the Walls of a Place, distant from 15 td so Foot one from another, which are advanced as much as is possible in rhe Ground, and joind to the height of the Cordon by Vaults co support the Way of the Rounds, and part of the Rampart, a$ also to fortifie the Wall, and strengthen the Ground ; nevertheless they are not ac present much used except in large Fortifications.

counterfugue.c: COUNTERFUGUE, in Musick, is when the Fugues proceed contrary to one another.

counterguardsorenvelopes.c: COUNTER-GUARDS or Envelopes , in Fortification, are large heaps of Earth in form of a Parapet raised above the Moat, before the Faces and the Point of the Bastion to preserve them ; and then they consist of two Faces, making an Angle Saliam and parallel with the Faces of the Bastion. If they are designed to cover one of the Faces of the Bastion, they are soaped like a DemiBastion, with a Parapet on the Face and Capital, but node on the Flank, which must lie open and be exposed to the Fire of the place: But there are few places now fortified after this manner by reason of the excessive Charge it requires.

countermand.c: COUNTERMAND, is where a thing formerly executed, is afterwards by some Acts or Ceremony madfc void by the Party that had first done it.

countermarch.c: COUNTER-MARCH, in the Art of War, signifies changing the Face or the W ings of a Battalion t and this is dbne either by Files or by G« j, COUNTERC O u c O u

countermarchbyfiles.c: COUNTER-MARCH by Files, >s when those Men that are in the Fsont of the Battalion go into the Bear.

countermarchbyranks.c: COUNTER-MARCH by Bankj, is when the Wings or Flanks of the Battalion change Ground with one another.

countermine.c: COUNTER MINE, in Fortification, is a Sub terraneous Passage made by the Besieged in search ot the Enemies Mine, to give Air thereto, to take away the Powder, or by any other means to frustrate tile effect of it, though it should even happen to be fired bv the Assailants.

counterpart.c: COUNTER-PART, a Term in Mustek, only denoting one Part to be opposite to another, as the Base is said to be the Counter-part of she treble.

counterpassant.c: COUNTER-PASSANT, when two Lions ate born in a Coat of Arms, and one appears to be passing or walking quite the contrary wjiy with the other, the Heralds call it by this Term Counter-Pass ant.

counterplea.c: COUNTER-PLEA, (in Common-Law) signifies that which the Demandant allegeth against a Tenant in Courtesie, or in Dower, who prayeth in aid of the King, or him who hath the Reversion, for his better defence.

counterpoint.c: COUNTER POINT, in Mustek, is a Term whereby is understood the old manner of composing Parts, before Notes of different Measure were invented ; which was, to set Pricks or Points one against another, to denote the several Concords j the Length or Measure of which Points was sung according to the quantity of the Words or Syllables whereto they are apply'd ; so that in regard that in composing our Descant we set Note against Note, as the Ancients did Point against Point ; the Term Counter-point is still retained in these Compositions.

countersailient.c: COUNTER-SAILIENT, is when two Beasts are born in a Coat of Arms in a Posture of leaping from each other, directly the contrary way,

counterscarp.c: COUNTERSCARP, in Fortification, is that side of the Ditch which is next the Camp, or properly the Talus that supports the Earth of the Covert-way ; although by this Term is often understood, the whole Covert-way with its Parapet and Glacis. And so it is to be understood, when tis said, The Enemy lodged themselves on the Counter, scarp. COUNTER Swallows Tally is an Our-work in Fortification, in the form of a single Tenarle, wider next the Place, i. e. at the Gorge than at the Head, or next the Campaign. The Sides of this Counter Swallows Tail are not so well flank’d from the Place, as thole of the true Swallows Tail, and therefore ’tis not so good.

countertenor.c: COUNTER-TENOR, one of the mean or middle Parts of Mustek, so called as it were oppo-i site to the Tenor.

countertripping.c: COUNTER-TRIPPING ; when two Staggs or other Beasts are born in a Coat of Arms tripping, (i. e.) in a walking posture, and the Head of one is to the Tail of the other, the Heralds say they are Counter Tripping.

counters.c: COUNTERS, are two Parts of a Ship ; the upper Counter is reckoned from the Gallery co the lower part of the strait piece of the Stern The lower Counter is between the Transom and sower part of the Gallery.

countinghouse.c: COUNTING-HOUSE , in the King’s Houfhold : See Green-Cloth.

countycourt.c: COUNTY-COURT,. is & Court held every Month, by the Sheriff , or his Deputy the XJnderSheriff.

couped.c: COUPED, is the Heralds word for any in an Escutcheon which is born cut clear and venly off, in opposition to its being torn off i wb, 1 , they call erased. Thus the Arms of Vlstet W" 1 all Baronets carry, is a dexter Hand Coupes u cut eft at the Wrist.

coupleclose.c: COUPLE Close, a Term in Heraldry, the 4th part of a Cheveron .- These are never j’ 0 '. but in Pairs, except a Chevron be between t‘ ,e . faith Guillim, but Bloom gives an Instance t0 1 contrary. , e

course.c: COURSE, in Navigation, is that Point ,°*L e Compass, or Coast of the Horizon, on whist' Ship is to be steer’d from Place to Place, or r^ ^ the Angle between the Bpmb-Line and the W dian. A

courses.c: COURSES, in a Ship, are her Mains*‘j Foresail ; when she sails under them only w' 1 g. lacing on any Bonnets, they say then Ihe g 0 ^ der a Pair of Courses. j.

courtofchivalry.c: COURT os Chivalry, or the tehs the Judges are the Lord High Constable Marshal of England. This Court is the F c y of Martial-Law, and the Earl Marstoal ly one of the Judges, but also to see done.

courtofpeculiars.c: COURT of Peculiars, is a Spirit ua £ held in such Parishes as are exempt from 0 pf diction of the Bishops, and .are peculiarly ing to the Archbishop os Canterbury.

courtofbequests.c: COURT of Bequests, is a Court of the same Nature with the Chancery, to it, being principally instituted so r f^ such Petitioners, as in conscionable Cal j,ad 5 Supplication co his Majesty, This Cow ^ fumed so great a Power to it self, lt,a s tabv burthensom and grievous, and therefore jg 1 away with some others, by a Statute and 17 Car. crank.c: CRANK, the Sea Term for a Ship that cannot bear her Sails, or can bear but a small Sail for sear of oversetting; and they say she is Cranks by the Ground, when she cannot be brought on Ground without danger of overthrowing her.

crapula.c: CRAPULA, is an Head-ach proceeding from too much Wine. Btauchard.

crasisingrammar.c: CRASJS in Grammar, is the same with Synercsis, and draws two Letters belonging to different Syllables, into pne Syllable as Vtment for Vehement.

crasis.c: CRASIS, pr Temper amentum, is a convenient Mixture,of qualities in an .Animal Body. Blanchard.

crater.c: CRATER, the Name pf one of the southern Constellations consisting of 11 Stars.

craticula.c: CRATICULA, is a ChymicaiInstrument made of Square Pieces of Iron, as thick as ones Finger, placed so ne«r one another in Acute Angles, that there’s half a Fingers space betwixt them, it is used in making pf Fires to keep up,the Coals. Blanched cream of Tartar, is Tartar boiled in a great deal of Water so that as much of it as can may be there dissolved, then the dissolution is pasted hoc .through Hippocrates his Sleeve, and about half the Liquor (being evaporated ; .the Remainder is set in a cool place, ana the Tartar will shoot into Chrystals, and some of it be like a Cream on the Top of the Water: This latter is properly the Cream of Tartar , and the dormer are Chrystals of Tartar, though both are of the same Nature and Use. Sometimes the Rust of Iron powdred is boiled in the Water along with the Tartar ; and then the Chrystals are passed Chalybeate Chrystals of Tartar.

crenyles.c: CRENYLES, in a Ship, are small Ropes spliced into the bolt-ropes of the Sails of the Main-Mast and Fore Malt; they are fastened to the bowling birdies,and are also to hold by, when a bonnet is sliaken off.

crepusculum.c: CREPUSCULUM, signifies Twilight, either Morning or Evening. See Twilight.

crescent.c: CRESCENT . the Heralds Term for an half Moon, which they draw of this Figure, and though it be fomeimes born as Coat Armour, yet is usually the distinguishing Mark of the a Brother, or Family from the First.

crest.c: CREST, in Heraldry signifies that Representation, whatever it be, whether Animal, VetegabJe, or other Artificial things, which is born on a wreath Cbeafeau, &c. on the Top of the Helmet in any Atcheivemenr. This they call also the Cognisance.

cribration.c: CRIBRATION, the Chymists word for sifting afiy Powder, or passing through a fine Sieve.

cribrumbenedictumantiquorum.c: CRIBRUM benedictum antiquorum, the Ancients fan lied two Cavities placed long ways in the Reins ; one uppermost wherein the serous Blood was poured from the Emulgent Arteries; another loweribost, which they fancied was distinguished with a certain Transverse Membrane full of little holes like a Sieve ; whence they called it Colatorium, a Strainer, and Benedictum Cribrum a blessed Sieve, through which they would have the Serum Percoiated into the Vrectcrs, and the good Blood stay behind for the Nourishment ot the Reins. Blanchard.

cricoarytnoides.c: CRICOARYTÆNOIDES, are Muscles which proceed from the Cartilage, called Cricoides laterally, and are inserted into the Aryttenoides, which whilst they draw the Aryt.cnois sidewise and outwardly, the opening or Rimula of the Larynx is Dilated. Blanchard.

cricoides.c: CRICOIDES, is the Cartilage of the Larynx or Windpipe, in fashion of a Ring.

cricothyroides.c: CRICOTHYROIDES, a pair of Muscles, which proceed from the Cartilage of the Larynx , like a Ring from the Fore-part of the Cricoides , and are terminated in that which is call’d the Scutiformis ; they Dilate the opening of the Larynx by moving a little obliquely, its use is to pull up the Annularis. CRIMNOIDES', or Crimnodes , is Urine with thick Sediments at the Bottom like Bran. Blanchard.

crisis.c: CRISIS, is a sudden change in a Disease, either towards a Recovery or Death. It sometimes signifies a Secretion of Humours; but is more frequently taken for a Judgment passed upon a Disease ; one Crisis is called perce ft, another imperfect, the perfect is that which frees the Patient perfectly from the Distemper; and it is either Salutary, or deadly. An imperfect Crisis , is that which does not clearly determine the Tendency of the Disease, but leaves Room for another Crisis ; and this is two-fold, either for the better, or for the worse, the former is that which does not quite take away the Disease, but enables the Patient to bear it better ; the latter is, when the Disease becomes more violent and dangerous. Blanchard. j

crownwork.c: CROWN-WORK.S, in Fortifications, are certain Bulwarks advanced toward the Field to gain some Hill or rising Ground, being composed of a spacious Gorge, and cwoWmgs that fall on theCwwr ter scarp near the Faces of the Bastion, so that they are defended by them, and present on the side of the Field, an entire Bastion between two DemiBastions, whose Faces look towards one another. Those Works also have their Half-Moens, and are raised only to take up or secure some large space of Ground, or to defend the Head. of a Camp when it is intrenched. CROWN’D Horn-wort^, is a lorn-wort^ with a Croxvn-veer^ before it.

crowfeet.c: CROW FEET, in a Ship, are small Lines or Ropes put through the Holes of the Dead Mens Eyes, arid divided by that means into 6 or 1 o, or sometimes more parts; they are of no use at all, but are there left hanging by the Boat Swain co make a shew of small Rigging • they are placed at the bottom of the Back-Stayr of the Forc-iopmast, Mizen-top-mast, and Gallant-rop-mast. There goes also a Rope divided into zor 4 Portions from the upper end of the Sprit-lad Top-mast to rhe ForeTojr mast Stay, which they call the Sprit-fail Top-sai! Crowfoot.

crowsfeet.c: CROWS-FEET, ( called also Caltrops and Chauste Trapes) are Irpns so made with 4 Points, of r, 3, or 4 Inches long, that which way soever they fall, one Point may be uppermost ; the shorter are to strow on Bridges, the longer On the Ground, to gall the Feet of a Body of Horse.

crucible.c: CRUCIBLE, is a Chymical Vessel made of Earth, and so tempered and baked as to endure the greatest Fire. They are used to melt Metals, to flux Minerals, Oars, &c, and are of this Figure. rr A French Crucible, A German Crucible, **2

crudity.c: CRUDITY, in Diseases, is when the Blood (as in continued Fevers) is not yet duly fermented, and brought to a right Consistence. Crudity ot the Stomach, is when Meat out of a Defect of Nourishment, or some other cause, is not rightly fermented and turned into Cliyje; and it is threefold, Apepfia , Bradypepfia, and Difpepsta ; of which in their proper places. Blanchard.

crura.c: CRURA, are the two Heads or beginnings of the Marrowy Substance of the Brain, called Medulla Oblongata. CRURA Medulla Oblongata , the Internal Substance of the two sides of the Cerebrum, gathered together as it were in two Bandles.

cruralartery.c: CRURAL Artery , by some said to be the Artery of the Thigh, among whose Muscles it divideth itself: It is a continuation of the Iliads Artery, which passing out of the Abdomen, and earring into the Thighs, it loses its former Name, and is called Cruralis. Besides some less remarkable Branches, before it come to the Ham, it fends forth the External and Internal Muscle ; under the Ham, it produces the two Poplitxa's, and somewhat lower the Surales. Afterwards the Trunk it self is divided into the Branches called Anterior and Posterior, and the last of these is also subdivided intb two smaller Branches which descend to the Foot.

cruralveinjtheblood.c: CRURAL Vein j the Blood is conveyed from the lower extremity of the Body by six Veins, called, The greater and smaller Ifcbia, Muscula, Poflitxa, and Sapbœna , which joining together compose the Trunk of the Crural Vein, which ascends to the Groin and ends in the Iliaca.

crureusorfemoreus.c: CRUREUS or Femoreus, is a Muscle of the Leg, so called from its Situation on the Bone of the Thigh, like the Musculus Branchixus, on that of the Arm ; its Origination is large and fleshy, being continued from between the greater and lesser Trochanter of the Thigh-bone forwards, to its lower part, that is, immediately above its Inferipr Appendix. It’s fleshy Fibres descend directly, and become perfectly Tendinous a little below the upper part of the Tendon of the Bectus, where it joyns with it, and the Tendons of the Vast us Extcrnus and Internus, which passes over the external part of the Palella, (or on each side of it) and is inserted to a Prominence at the Superior and fbre-part of the Tibia $ it helps to extend the Tibia.

crusormagnuspes.c: CRUS or Magnus Pes, is all that part of the Body, which reaches from the Buttocks down to the end of the Toes; and it is divided into the Thigh, Leg, and Foot. Blanchard. CRUST A Lailea, is a Species of Achor, Scurf, or crusty Scab; only with this difference, that an Achor insects only the Head; but this not only the Face, but almost the whole Body of an Infant at the time of its first sucking. Blanchard, Crusta Laftea turns white, but Achors have only one Colour.

crustaceous.c: CRUSTACEOUS, Shell Fishes, are such as Lobsters, Crabs, Craw-fishes, &c. which are covered with Shells, consisting of several Pieces and Joints, and which usually are softer too than those of the Testaceous Shell-fishes ; which are all entirely of one piece, and usually much harder, thicker, and stronger than the former; as the Oyster, Scollop, Cockle, &c.

crustula.c: CRUSTULA, is the same as Ecchynoma in the Eye, being a descent of Blood from the Arteries into the Tunica Conjunctiva, occasioned by a wound, streak, G?c.

crymodes.c: CRYMODES, is a cold shivering Fever, but many times accompanied with an Inflammation of the inner parts, Blanchard.

crysorchis.c: CRYSORCHIS, is an absconding of the Testicles in the Belly. Blanchard. Men it is shaped like a Lens, or Convex Olast,E riles thicker in the Middle than at the Edges Humour is the least of ail the three, but is more Solid than any of them, and is cloathed ' vit a small Membrane of its own, called Arantt, reason of its thinness, like to a Spider’s Web.

curatio.c: CURATIO, is a right way or method of finding out by Symptoms and Indications, proper Remedies for any Disease, in order to the recovery of Health. Blanchard.

curiaclaudenda.c: CURIA Claudenda, is a Writ that lieth against him that should fence and close up his Ground, if he refuse or defer to do it.

cursitor.c: CURSITOR, is an Officer or Clerk belonging to the Chancery, that maketh out Original Writs •• They are called also Clerks of the Course ; and there be of these twenty lour in number, which have allotted to each of them several Shires, in which they make out such Original Writs, as are by the Subject required, and are a Corporation of themselves.

curtain.c: CURTAIN, in Fortification, is the Front of the Wall of a Fortify’d Place between two Bastions ; or the longest straight Line that runs about the Rampart, drawn from one Flank to the other, and bordered with a Parapet five Foot high, behind which the Soldiers stand to sire upon the Covert-way and into the Moat. Besiegers seldom carry on their Attacks against the Curtain, because ’tis the best flank’d of any Part.

curtationofaplanet.c: CURTATION of a Planet, in Astronomy, according to some, is a little part cut off from the Line of his Interval or Distance from the Sun.
